posts.title: Wind on a sheeted façade is a temporary works load — not a weather inconvenience
posts.excerpt: ABC News and 7NEWS, 27 September 2026: a large section of scaffolding at a demolition site on Wattle Street, Ultimo, Sydney, fell onto parked cars on Saturday evening. SafeWork NSW said no one was injured, inspectors attended, and a prohibition notice was issued. CCTV shows strong winds. CROSS-UK Report 1413 (19 August 2025) asks whether out-of-service wind loads used for temporary works have been underestimated against BS EN 1991-1-6.
posts.linkedinReady:
A sheeted scaffold on a public street is not a weather inconvenience. It is a temporary works structure with a wind load and a third-party risk.

ABC News and 7NEWS reported on 27 September 2026 that a large section of scaffolding at a demolition site on Wattle Street, Ultimo, Sydney, fell onto parked cars on Saturday evening. SafeWork NSW said no one was injured. Inspectors attended. A prohibition notice was issued to the site managers. CCTV showed the scaffolding giving way in strong winds and narrowly missing people in the street. The same site had a wall collapse in August that seriously injured two men. SafeWork NSW is investigating. Causes are not established in the public reporting.

That is the public face of a load case every UK contractor already has on the register: façade scaffold, debris net or sheeting, ties, and wind. CROSS-UK Report 1413 (19 August 2025) is the UK technical companion. A reporter asked whether out-of-service wind loads taken from NASC TG20, NASC TG30 or BS 5975 comply with BS EN 1991-1-6:2005, and whether temporary works wind loads have been underestimated for years. The report is a question for the industry, not a finding on any named site.

For contractors:
- Register sheeted and debris-netted façades as temporary works, including demolition protection and pavement gantries.
- Do not treat TG20 as automatic cover once sheeting, advertising, or extra boards go on. That is a design brief, not a catalogue pick.
- Check ties, foundations and the existing façade they fix to — the same lesson as CROSS 1539 on props and existing structure.
- Have a wind action: inspect after gales, drop sheeting if the procedure says so, keep the public exclusion zone real.
- A prohibition notice after the event is not a temporary works procedure.

Educational only. Not for construction. Subject to the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: On 27 September 2026 ABC News reported that scaffolding at a building site on Wattle Street, Ultimo, in inner Sydney, partially collapsed onto parked cars on Saturday evening just before 18:45 local time. SafeWork NSW said no one was injured. Inspectors attended the site and issued regulatory notices, including a prohibition notice to the site managers. ABC and 7NEWS both reported that CCTV showed the scaffolding giving way in strong winds and narrowly missing people in the street. 7NEWS quoted Fire and Rescue NSW describing a large section of scaffolding across traffic lanes, about 20 metres long and 10 metres high, with two parked cars caught underneath. A neighbour told ABC there was wind, a loud sound of metal on the road, and that she believed the front structure and demolition protection panels were not secure. Macroview Projects, named by ABC as managing the development, had been contacted for comment at the time of publication. SafeWork NSW is investigating. No official finding on cause has been published.

ABC reported that a wall and roof at the same Ultimo site collapsed onto a nearby petrol station last month, seriously injuring two men, one in his 60s and one in his 30s. Work had only recently resumed after being halted. The building had been a rehearsal studio and was approved for demolition for a multi-storey mixed-use development. Those facts are from the same ABC article. They do not prove the cause of Saturday's scaffold failure.

CROSS-UK Safety Report 1413, published 19 August 2025, is titled Are temporary works wind loads underestimated? A reporter said that out-of-service wind loads calculated from NASC TG20, NASC TG30 or BS 5975 for temporary works designs do not comply with BS EN 1991-1-6:2005, and asked whether temporary works wind loads have been underestimated for the past 30 years. The reporter stated that BS 5975:2019 and BS 5975-2:2024 adopt Clause NA.8.2 of BS EN 12812:2008, aligned with superseded CP 3 Chapter V-2 and BS 5973, and recommended amendment of BS 5975-2:2024, the NA clause, and user-selectable annual probability of exceedance in TG20 and TG30. That report is a published industry concern. It is not a finding on the Ultimo site and must not be read as one.

body.h: Why it matters for UK contractors
body.p: Façade scaffold, pavement gantries, debris net, sheeting, advertising banners and demolition catch systems are temporary works. Wind is a design load. The public highway is part of the risk. BS 5975-1:2024 puts the item on the register, names a TWC, requires a brief that states sheeting and exposure, and requires inspection and a permit before the structure is loaded or left in service over a street. TG20 covers defined standard scaffolds. Once you add sheeting, extra boards, or a non-standard tie pattern, you have left the catalogue and you need a design. The existing wall you tie into is part of the same scheme.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Register sheeted façades, demolition protection and pavement scaffolds before erection.
State sheeting, debris net, banners and boarded lifts in the design brief.
Do not assume a TG20 compliance sheet covers a sheeted or netted elevation.
Check ties and the existing structure they fix to. Opening-up if the façade is suspect.
Define a wind action in the method: inspect after gales, drop or reef sheeting if required, keep exclusion zones.
Provisional category only — confirm under the project temporary works procedure.
Hold points: brief, design or TG20 check, tie inspection, handover, inspection after severe weather, no public access under an uninspected elevation.
Do not proceed until reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

body.p: Educational briefing only. Not for construction. Not a design, not a check and not a permit. Subject to the project temporary works procedure. Facts from ABC News 27 September 2026, 7NEWS 27 September 2026, and CROSS-UK Report 1413 (19 August 2025). Confirm against those pages. No finding of cause is made here. posts.title: Props that can take the load are still unsafe if the slab they sit on cannot
posts.excerpt: CROSS-UK Report 1539 (14 May 2026): temporary props for replacing a defective RC column in a multi-storey block were already installed. The props could carry over 1,165 kN characteristic / about 1,590 kN design. Opening-up showed the existing beams and slabs would fail in bending and shear. The drawing was For Approval and pushed the existing-structure check onto the client. HSE 15 June 2026 Paxton House: temporary platforms with no design and no calculated safe load collapsed onto a drilling operative.
posts.linkedinReady:
A pair of heavy-duty props is not a temporary works scheme if nobody has checked the slab and beams they sit on.

CROSS-UK Report 1539 (14 May 2026) describes a defective RC column at the base of a multi-storey block of flats. Characteristic load over 1,165 kN. Design load about 1,590 kN. Props were already on site. The drawing was marked For Approval and carried a caveat that the client must confirm the existing structure could take the extra load. The props themselves could carry the force. Opening-up then showed the existing beams and slabs would fail in bending and shear under the redistributed load. The Reporter designed a more complex scheme and a written method. Without that work, a significant part of the building was at risk of collapse.

The Expert Panel called it a failure of the temporary works procedure: TWC and checker missing on a significant structure, and a brief that designed the kit in isolation from the load path to a foundation.

HSE June 2026 Paxton House prosecution is the same lesson from the other end. Temporary wooden platforms under core-drilled openings had no design and no calculated safe load. Debris accumulated. The platform collapsed onto Steve Zschoch. Neck and back fractures. Two contractors fined under CDM 2015.

For contractors: the brief must include the existing structure. Caveats on a For Approval drawing do not transfer the check. Register the scheme, name the TWC, get opening-up and a load-path check before anyone takes a column out.

Educational only. Not for construction. Subject to the project temporary works procedure.

#TemporaryWorks #CROSSUK #HSE #Propping #BS5975 #CDM2015

body.p: CROSS-UK published Safety Report 1539 on 14 May 2026. A Reporter was asked to advise on temporary works to remove a defective reinforced concrete column at the base of a multi-storey block of flats and replace it with a new steel column. Estimated characteristic load on the column was over 1,165 kN and estimated design load approximately 1,590 kN. On arrival, heavy-duty props were already installed. The prop designer had left a drawing showing pairs of props under the beams and slab either side of the column. Status: For Approval. A note on the drawing said the client must be assured the scheme was safe and suitable and that, if the system created additional loads on an existing structure, the structure could safely support those loads. The props themselves could take the required forces. There was no evidence the existing structure had been checked. Opening-up showed the existing beams and slabs were not strong enough to transfer load from the props to the concrete column above and would fail in bending and shear. The Reporter designed a more complex temporary works system and a written method statement. Without those additional works the Reporter considered it likely that a significant part of the building would have collapsed.

The CROSS Expert Panel described the report as worrying and as a failure of the temporary works procedure that should have been in place, with a Temporary Works Coordinator and checking engineer appointed on what sounded like a significant structure. When temporary works support an existing structure, a viable load path must be understood and verified from the point of application through to a suitable foundation. Designing props in isolation creates unsafe assumptions if the surrounding structure has not been assessed. Beams that previously took one floor into the column may now have to carry shear from more floors. The Panel pointed to CROSS Report 1459 on inadequate propping of an existing timber beam. Competent engineers should recognise an incomplete brief and advise accordingly.

On 15 June 2026 HSE published the outcome of a prosecution after a temporary platform collapse at Paxton House in the City of London on 23 February 2024. Roots Contractors Limited had instructed carpenters to build temporary wooden platforms under openings cut through five concrete floors to form a service riser, to collect 16 kg cores and debris. Steve Zschoch of Diacutt Limited was cutting on the third floor under one platform when it collapsed with uncleared concrete. He sustained fractures to his neck and back and a bleed on the brain. HSE found no design and no calculated safe load. An inspection form was completed by someone who was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. Roots Contractors Limited pleaded guilty to CDM 2015 Regulation 16(2) and was fined 19333 pounds plus 5548 pounds costs on 11 June 2026. Diacutt Limited pleaded guilty to CDM 2015 Regulation 15(2) and was fined 13000 pounds plus 5548 pounds costs.

Column replacement, riser cutting, crash decks and propping of existing floors are temporary works. Kit capacity is only one line in the check. The existing slab, beam, wall and foundation that receive the load are part of the same scheme. BS 5975-1:2024 puts the item on the register, names a TWC and TWS, requires a design brief that includes the existing structure, and requires an independent check and permit before load is taken or a column is removed. A For Approval drawing that caves the existing-structure check back to the client is not a completed design.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Register column replacement, floor openings, crash decks and propping of existing structure before the first prop is stood or the first core is cut.
Issue a design brief that requires the existing load path to be verified.
Do not accept a For Approval drawing whose only existing-structure clause is a client caveat.
Opening-up before load. If the structure cannot take the prop loads, redesign.
Provisional category only — to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

Hold points: brief accepted, existing structure checked, scheme checked, inspection before load, permit-to-load, no one under loaded platforms, debris clearance to a stated limit, permit before column removal.
Completing a form is not the same as being the TWC.
Do not proceed until reviewed and accepted by the competent person under the project temporary works procedure.

Facts from CROSS-UK Report 1539 (14 May 2026) and HSE Media Centre 15 June 2026. Confirm against those pages. AI-assisted drafting requires competent review before use on site.

posts.title: Do not copy CIRIA C761 shear enhancement onto the tension side of a piled crane base
posts.excerpt: CROSS-UK Report 1552 (29 June 2026) flags Worked Example 3 in CIRIA C761. Shear enhancement cannot be used where both the crane leg and the pile are in tension.
